4.1 — The Enemy: Patrol

The turret never moves. This enemy walks a beat with nobody at the keyboard — a route it can repeat forever, defined by objects you place in the scene.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make an enemy follow a patrol route?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The enemy should walk a beat — back and forth, forever, with nobody at the keyboard. "Make the enemy patrol" is the whole feature, and at this moment the enemy is a picture with an empty script on it: it has never moved once.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Write the route down as a list of placesOne serialized List<Transform> slot on the prefab. Each entry is a Transform you place in the scene and drag in — a route of two points today, five later, without a line of new code.Read: the [SerializeField] private List<Transform> row of this lesson's table, and the serialized-field rule from 1.3.
  2. Remember which point it is walking towardOne int — an index into the list, not a Transform. It starts at 0 and it is the only thing in the file that changes when the enemy turns around.Read: the field declarations from 1.3, and the int you used for WalkDir in 1.6.
  3. Move toward that point at a constant speedVector3.MoveTowards() with speed * Time.deltaTime as the step. It refuses to overshoot, so the enemy lands exactly on the point instead of sailing past it.Read: the Vector3.MoveTowards() row of this lesson's table, and Time.deltaTime from 1.5.
  4. write this partRead: the Vector3.Distance() row in the quick reference, and List<T>.Count in the scripting reference.

Three of those four parts are work you have already done: a serialized field is 1.3, a number that changes is 1.3, and a distance compared against a threshold is 3.1. Only one part has no precedent at all: a route has an END. Every number this game has remembered so far was allowed to grow forever, and this one is not — the moment it equals the size of the list, reading the list throws.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make an enemy patrol" cannot be looked up. "Move an object toward a position at a constant speed" can.

Your turn

The table prices three ways to define a route. Which did you choose, and what does your choice cost you — in your own words, not the table's?

The enemy's whole memory is one int. What does it index, and what happens on the first frame it equals patrolPoints.Count?

In the Editor ~20 min
  1. Hierarchy → count the MobileEnemy instances in the Overworld: four, against exactly one Coin. Write the count down before you move anything.
  2. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/MobileEnemy, and select the prefab asset, not an instance in the scene. Its root is tagged Enemy, carries a Capsule Collider 2D and a Rigidbody 2D set to Dynamic with Gravity Scale 0. Read those: today's movement does not use the body, but 4.3 will, and you should know it is already there.
  3. Hierarchy → MobileEnemy → Detection Radius: a child with a Circle Collider 2D, Is Trigger ticked. That is next lesson's aggro radius — leave it alone today, and notice that the project wired it before it wrote the script that uses it.
  4. Hierarchy → right-click → Create Empty, twice, in the Overworld. Rename them PatrolPointA and PatrolPointB, and place them with the Move tool in the Scene view at the two ends of a beat that makes sense in the level. They are positions and nothing else.
  5. Hierarchy → one enemy instance, Inspector → Enemy Controller → Patrol Points: set Size to 2, then drag the two empty objects into the two slots. Repeat per instance if three enemies should walk three different routes.
  6. Once the code half is done — Game view → press Play and watch one enemy walk the loop. Then add a third point to the list while Play is running and watch it take the longer route — nothing in the script changed.
  7. Console → if you see ArgumentOutOfRangeException, the list is empty, or the index ran past its end. Check Size in the Inspector before you check the code.

Read the three rows below before you write anything. All three are the same four parts in different clothes, and only what the field remembers differs — a place, an index, or a limit.

The rowWhat it remembers, and how it turnsWhat it costs you
A leash from the spawn point The position it started at, plus how far it may wander. It measures the drift with Vector3.Distance() and flips the stored sign once that exceeds the leash. No scene setup at all, and the beat follows the enemy wherever you drag it. But it is always a straight line centred on the spawn point, and the turn is noticed only after the enemy has moved — so it always overshoots by up to one frame of travel.
A list of placed waypoints — this project A List<Transform> wired in the Inspector, plus an int remembering which entry it is heading for. It walks to that point, advances the index, and wraps to 0 at the end. You must place and wire every point, per instance, and guard the wrap — an index one past the end is an exception. In exchange the route is as long as you like without new code.
Two absolute bounds Two numbers, a minimum and a maximum, and a sign the movement multiplies by. The simplest maths and the most brittle. Those bounds are world coordinates, so moving the enemy leaves its beat behind and a copied prefab turns on frame one. Let the sign ever reach 0 and the walk stops for good.

Socratic: Designing a Beat

  1. Which of the three route definitions fits an enemy you will place four or five times across a map and keep nudging while you design the level? What does your choice cost you?
  2. The leash approach stores the position the enemy started at. Which lifecycle method must save it, and what would the enemy do if you saved it every frame instead?
  3. The enemy's whole memory is one int that counts up. Why is an index enough to define a route — and what would go wrong with a bool such as isGoingRight once the route has five points?
In the CodeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I make an enemy follow a patrol route?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs. The enemy ships as a stub: an EnemyController on a prefab with a body, standing in the Overworld four times over. Today it gets a route, an index into that route, and the line that sends the index back to the start.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Declare the route and the index

The using goes at the top of the file with the others; the rest goes in the class body, with your fields.

// EnemyController.cs — the top of the file, above the class.
using System.Collections.Generic;

// EnemyController.cs — class body, above Start(), with your other fields.
    [SerializeField] private List<Transform> patrolPoints = new List<Transform>();
    int patrolNumber = 0;
    Vector3 targetPosition;

    float speed = 2;
  1. 2The namespace List<> lives in. Unity adds using UnityEngine; for you when the script is created; this one you add yourself.Without it, List is an unknown name. The compiler error points at the type — "The type or namespace name List could not be found" — which reads like the list is wrong when the only thing missing is one line at the top of the file.
  2. 5The route. A list of Transforms — each entry is an object you placed in the scene and dragged into the Inspector slot. [SerializeField] is what puts the slot there at all.= new List<Transform>() is not decoration. Without it the field starts as null, and the first thing your code will do is ask it how many points it has — a NullReferenceException instead of an empty list. An empty list is a route with no points, which is a bug you can see; a null list is a crash that reads like a code fault. (Unity fills a serialized list for you once you press Play with one wired, which is exactly why the difference is invisible until it isn't.)
  3. 6The memory. Which entry in the list the enemy is walking toward right now. 0 is the first point; the line that moves it is the gap in step 3.
  4. 7The spot in the world the enemy is walking to this frame — read out of the list so the movement line does not have to say patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position twice.
  5. 9How fast it walks, in units per second.

Step 2Seed the first destination

Start() runs once, before Update() has ever run.

// EnemyController.cs — inside Start().
        targetPosition = patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position;
  1. 2Reads entry 0 of the list and keeps its position. Update() will overwrite this every frame, so the line is really a declaration of intent: the enemy starts walking toward the first point.This line is where an empty list announces itself. With nothing wired, patrolPoints[0] does not exist, and the Console fills with ArgumentOutOfRangeException before the first frame is drawn. The exception names this line, and the bug is in the Inspector.

Step 3Arrive, advance, wrap, walk

One Update() doing four things in order. Only one of them is new.

// EnemyController.cs — inside Update().
        if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position) < .1f)
        {
            patrolNumber += 1;
            ______________________________
        }

        targetPosition = patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position;

        float step = speed * Time.deltaTime;
        transform.position = Vector3.MoveTowards(transform.position, targetPosition, step);
  1. 2The arrival test: the distance check from 3.1, against a threshold of a tenth of a unit. True on every frame the enemy is standing close enough to the point it was walking toward.
  2. 4The turn: the index moves to the next point in the list. This is the whole reason the enemy can walk a beat with nobody at the keyboard — a player turns because a key was pressed, and the enemy has no keys.
  3. Your turn5The wrap. The index has just been incremented, so it might now point past the end of the list — write the line that sends it back to the first point when it does.Ask two questions in one condition: has the index reached the number of points in the list? If so, what should it be instead of that number? The list can tell you its own size.Leave this out and the enemy crashes at the end of its route. The next line reads patrolPoints[patrolNumber], and an index equal to Count is one past the last entry — ArgumentOutOfRangeException, every frame, forever. A list does not loop; the number that walks it has to. This is the difference between a route and a count.
  4. 8Re-read the destination from the list. On most frames this is the same point as last frame; on the frame the enemy arrived, it is the next one.
  5. 10How far to travel this frame: speed is per second, so the frame's duration turns it into per frame — the multiplication from 1.5.
  6. 11Moves the object toward the destination by exactly one step, stopping on the point rather than passing it.MoveTowards() cannot overshoot. A velocity line would travel step units in the direction of the point even when the point is only half a step away — the enemy would jitter past the waypoint and the arrival test would flicker. Because the third argument is already a distance, this line takes speed * Time.deltaTime rather than speed alone. And it moves the Transform, not the body — the same shortcut the Player took in 1.4 before 2.2 replaced it. That is a debt, not an accident: the body is still there, because 4.3 needs the trigger and 4.6 needs something to hit.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The gap is the wrap, and it is the one idea in this lesson with nothing earlier to copy. The file above writes it across three lines; a single-line if (patrolNumber == patrolPoints.Count) patrolNumber = 0; is the same program. Your waypoints, your speed and your threshold are yours; the shape is what has to match.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class EnemyController : MonoBehaviour
{
    float speed = 2;

    // The route: objects placed in the scene and dragged into the Inspector.
    [SerializeField] private List<Transform> patrolPoints = new List<Transform>();

    // The memory: which entry the enemy is walking toward.
    int patrolNumber = 0;

    Vector3 targetPosition;

    void Start()
    {
        targetPosition = patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position) < .1f)
        {
            patrolNumber += 1;

            // The wrap: a list does not loop, so the index has to.
            if (patrolNumber == patrolPoints.Count)
            {
                patrolNumber = 0;
            }
        }

        targetPosition = patrolPoints[patrolNumber].position;

        float step = speed * Time.deltaTime;
        transform.position = Vector3.MoveTowards(transform.position, targetPosition, step);
    }
}

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare the three ways to define a route, name the one this project uses, and defend it
  • Explain why the route lives in a serialized list rather than in two hard-coded positions
  • Point at the one field that is your enemy's whole memory of where it is going, and the line that changes it
  • Explain what happens without the wrap, and name the exception it produces
  • Say what Vector3.MoveTowards() refuses to do that a velocity line does, and why the third argument is speed * Time.deltaTime
  • Say how many enemies and how many coins the Overworld shipped with
  • Commit and push
